name: Olive Oil
aka: Extra virgin olive oil, EVOO, Olea europaea
summary: Extra virgin olive oil is anti-inflammatory (oleocanthal acts like low-dose ibuprofen) and cardioprotective; the PREDIMED trial found a Mediterranean diet with EVOO cut cardiovascular events by about 30%.
how: 2-4 tablespoons daily of cold-pressed EVOO in food; apply directly to skin; warm drops in ear for earache.
safety: 120 cal/tablespoon. Never use in ear if the eardrum is perforated. Olive allergy possible; large amounts are mildly laxative.
origin: Hippocrates called it 'the great healer'; Dioscorides used it for skin, ears, and as a base for ointments.

name: Oregano Oil
summary: Carvacrol and thymol show broad antimicrobial and antifungal activity in vitro (including MRSA and Candida), with one trial supporting oregano capsules against intestinal parasites; human data remain limited.
how: Enteric-coated capsules standardized to 50-80% carvacrol for 7-14 day courses; 1-2 drops diluted in carrier oil topically; 2-3 drops in hot water for steam inhalation.
safety: Never take undiluted essential oil internally (burns mucous membranes). Avoid in pregnancy (uterine stimulant). May interact with blood thinners. Skin irritant; mint-family allergy possible. Not for long-term daily use.
origin: Dioscorides prescribed oregano for respiratory and digestive problems; Hippocrates used it as an antiseptic.

name: Thyme
summary: Thyme extract is an approved bronchitis and productive-cough treatment in Germany; a clinical trial of thyme-ivy combination significantly reduced cough frequency and severity in acute bronchitis.
how: Steep 1-2 tsp dried thyme in 8 oz boiling water 10 minutes; 2-3 cups daily during illness, with honey. Thyme-honey infusion or standardized cough syrups also used.
safety: Very safe as culinary herb and tea. Do not ingest undiluted essential oil. High doses may slow clotting - caution with anticoagulants. Avoid therapeutic doses in pregnancy; mint-family allergy possible.
origin: Galen and Dioscorides recommended thyme as an expectorant; Romans burned it to purify rooms.

name: Rosemary
summary: Rosemary aroma measurably improved cognitive performance and mood in a controlled study (1,8-cineole detected in plasma); carnosic and rosmarinic acids are potent antioxidants with preclinical neuroprotective effects.
how: Tea: 1 tsp dried rosemary in 8 oz hot water, 5-10 minutes. Use freely in cooking. Infuse fresh rosemary in olive oil for sore-muscle massage; diffuse the essential oil for focus.
safety: Culinary amounts very safe. Large medicinal doses may raise blood pressure - caution in hypertension. May worsen seizure disorders. Avoid large doses in pregnancy. Do not ingest the essential oil.
origin: Dioscorides used it for digestive and liver complaints; Greek students wore rosemary garlands for memory.

name: Chamomile
summary: A University of Pennsylvania RCT showed chamomile extract significantly reduced generalized anxiety symptoms, with benefit sustained over 38 weeks; apigenin binds benzodiazepine receptors and bisabolol aids wound healing.
how: Tea: 1 tbsp dried flowers in 8 oz boiling water, covered, 5-10 minutes; 1-3 cups daily. Anxiety trials used 220-1100 mg/day standardized extract. Cooled tea or cream applied to irritated skin.
safety: Allergy risk with ragweed/Asteraceae sensitivity. May increase effects of sedatives and blood thinners (warfarin). Stop before surgery.
origin: Prescribed by Dioscorides, Galen and Hippocrates; Egyptians dedicated it to the sun god Ra.

name: Lavender
summary: Oral lavender oil (Silexan) 80 mg/day matched lorazepam for generalized anxiety in rigorous RCTs without sedation or dependence, and a 2019 meta-analysis confirmed anxiolytic effects.
how: Silexan capsules 80 mg daily is the most studied form. Aromatherapy: 3-5 drops in a diffuser or 1-2 on the pillow. Tea: 1-2 tsp dried buds, 5-10 minutes. Dilute oil for temples or minor burns.
safety: Oral oil can cause burping/nausea; may enhance sedative drugs. Topical oil can cause contact dermatitis. Possible weak estrogenic effect - caution in hormone-sensitive conditions. Do not swallow raw essential oil.
origin: Dioscorides prescribed it for chest complaints; Romans bathed in it (Latin lavare, to wash).

name: Fennel
summary: A randomized trial found fennel seed oil emulsion significantly reduced infantile colic, and fennel extract matched mefenamic acid for menstrual pain; Commission E approves it for dyspepsia and GI spasms.
how: Crush 1-2 tsp seeds, steep in 8 oz boiling water 10 minutes, drink after meals. Chew half a teaspoon of seeds for gas. Commercial fennel gripe water for infant colic.
safety: Estrogenic - avoid therapeutic doses in estrogen-sensitive cancers. Allergy possible (celery-carrot-mugwort syndrome). Do not give concentrated essential oil to infants. Caution with large doses in pregnancy.
origin: Hippocrates and Dioscorides used fennel for digestion and lactation; Greek athletes ate it for stamina.

name: Peppermint
summary: Enteric-coated peppermint oil is among the best-evidenced herbal treatments for IBS, with meta-analyses of 12 RCTs showing reduced overall symptoms and abdominal pain; topical 10% oil matched acetaminophen for tension headache.
how: IBS: enteric-coated capsules 0.2-0.4 mL, 30-60 minutes before meals, 2-3x daily. Tea: 1 tsp dried leaf in 8 oz water 5-7 minutes. Headache: dilute oil applied to temples.
safety: Non-enteric capsules cause heartburn by relaxing the esophageal sphincter; avoid in severe GERD. Not for infants (menthol can impair breathing). May interact with CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 substrates.
origin: Dioscorides prescribed mint for stomach complaints and hiccups; Pliny recorded over 40 uses.

name: Valerian Root
summary: Systematic reviews find valerian modestly improves subjective sleep quality with few side effects; valerenic acid modulates GABA-A receptors. It works best with consistent use over 2-4 weeks, not as a single dose.
how: Standardized extract 300-600 mg, 30 minutes to 2 hours before bed. Tea: 2-3 g dried root steeped 10-15 minutes (unpleasant taste; often blended with lemon balm). Tincture 1-2 mL at night.
safety: Do not combine with alcohol, benzodiazepines or other sedatives without supervision. May cause morning grogginess. Stop 2 weeks before surgery (anesthesia interaction). Rare liver injury reports; limited data beyond 4-6 weeks.
origin: Dioscorides called it 'phu'; Galen prescribed it specifically for insomnia by the 2nd century CE.

name: St. John's Wort
summary: A Cochrane Review of 29 RCTs (5,489 patients) found St. John's Wort superior to placebo and comparable to SSRIs for mild-to-moderate depression with fewer side effects; hyperforin inhibits monoamine reuptake.
how: 300 mg three times daily, standardized to 0.3% hypericin or 2-5% hyperforin; effects emerge after 4-6 weeks. Red oil (flowering tops in olive oil, 4-6 weeks) topically for minor wounds and burns.
safety: CRITICAL: potent CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inducer - reduces effectiveness of oral contraceptives, warfarin, cyclosporine, HIV protease inhibitors, some chemotherapy, digoxin, theophylline. Never combine with SSRIs/SNRIs/MAOIs (serotonin syndrome). Causes photosensitivity. Not for severe depression or bipolar disorder; always tell your physician.
origin: Dioscorides used it for sciatica and burns; harvested around the feast of St. John, June 24.

name: Milk Thistle
summary: Silymarin is a well-studied liver protectant: IV silibinin is Europe's standard antidote for Amanita mushroom poisoning, and a meta-analysis found milk thistle lowered ALT and AST in fatty liver disease.
how: 140-420 mg silymarin daily in 2-3 divided doses with meals, standardized to 70-80% silymarin. Tea extracts poorly (silymarin is not water-soluble); phytosome forms absorb better.
safety: Well tolerated; mild diarrhea or bloating possible. Possible weak estrogenic effect - caution in hormone-sensitive conditions. May lower blood sugar (monitor if diabetic) and may interact with CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 drugs. Asteraceae allergy possible.
origin: Dioscorides described it for snake bites; Pliny recommended the juice with honey to 'carry off bile'.

name: Garlic
summary: A meta-analysis of 12 RCTs showed aged garlic extract lowered systolic blood pressure by about 8.3 mmHg in hypertensive patients; garlic also modestly reduces total and LDL cholesterol and allicin is broadly antimicrobial.
how: Crush 1-2 raw cloves and rest 10 minutes before eating (allows allicin to form). Aged garlic extract 600-1200 mg/day is the best-studied supplement. Add garlic late in cooking.
safety: Increases bleeding risk - stop 7-10 days before surgery; interacts with warfarin, antiplatelet drugs and saquinavir (HIV). Causes GI upset, heartburn, odor. May lower blood sugar. Raw garlic on skin can cause chemical burns.
origin: Hippocrates prescribed it for pulmonary complaints; Roman soldiers ate it for stamina.

name: Dandelion
summary: A human pilot study confirmed dandelion leaf extract increases urinary frequency and volume, and unlike drug diuretics it is naturally potassium-rich; root shows bile-stimulating and hepatoprotective activity in animals.
how: Leaf tea (diuretic): 1-2 tsp dried leaf in 8 oz boiling water 10 minutes, 2-3 cups daily. Root decoction (liver/digestion): simmer 1-2 tsp 10-15 minutes. Roasted root as coffee substitute; young leaves in salad.
safety: Avoid with Asteraceae allergy. Do not use with bile duct obstruction or gallstones without supervision. May interact with diuretics, lithium, diabetes drugs and blood thinners. Harvest only from pesticide-free areas.
origin: Used by Greco-Roman physicians as a digestive bitter and diuretic; Galen called it a liver remedy.

name: Stinging Nettle
summary: A double-blind study found freeze-dried nettle leaf effective for allergic rhinitis in 58% vs 37% on placebo, and multiple European trials support nettle root for benign prostatic hyperplasia (EMA and Commission E approved).
how: Leaf tea: 2-3 tsp dried leaf in 8 oz boiling water 10-15 minutes, 2-3 cups daily. Allergies: freeze-dried leaf capsules 300-600 mg at symptom onset. BPH: nettle root (not leaf) extract 300-600 mg daily.
safety: May interact with blood thinners, blood pressure drugs, diuretics, lithium and diabetes medications. Avoid in pregnancy (possible uterine stimulant). Always cook or dry before eating. Get urinary symptoms medically evaluated to rule out prostate cancer.
origin: Dioscorides used nettle for nosebleeds and as a diuretic; soldiers flogged arthritic joints with it.

name: Vinegar
summary: Vinegar taken before a high-carb meal improved postprandial insulin sensitivity by 19-34% in insulin-resistant subjects, and a 2021 meta-analysis confirmed reductions in fasting glucose and HbA1c; weight effects are modest.
how: Dilute 1-2 tbsp raw apple cider vinegar in 8 oz water before meals. Oxymel: equal parts ACV and raw honey, 1 tbsp in warm water for cough and sore throat. Never drink undiluted.
safety: Undiluted vinegar erodes tooth enamel - dilute, use a straw, rinse. Irritates esophagus and stomach, especially with GERD or ulcers. May interact with diuretics and insulin/diabetes drugs; chronic high doses lower potassium. Avoid with gastroparesis.
origin: Hippocrates used oxymel for coughs and wounds; Roman soldiers drank posca, water with vinegar.

name: Parsley
summary: Clinical data are limited, but Commission E approves parsley herb and root for flushing therapy in urinary tract complaints; it is exceptionally nutrient-dense in vitamin K, vitamin C and folate, with anti-inflammatory apigenin.
how: Tea: a generous handful of fresh parsley (or 2 tsp dried) steeped in 8 oz boiling water 10 minutes. Eat fresh parsley liberally as food. Seed tea is a stronger diuretic requiring caution.
safety: Avoid therapeutic doses in pregnancy (seeds and oil are traditional abortifacients; apiol is the concern) - culinary amounts are fine. High vitamin K may interact with blood thinners. Seed oil can be nephrotoxic in large doses; high oxalate - caution with kidney stones.
origin: Dioscorides prescribed parsley as a diuretic; Galen used it for kidney and bladder stones.

name: Rooibos
summary: Rooibos polyphenols aspalathin and nothofagin are potent antioxidants; a human study showed improved lipid profile and redox status in adults at cardiovascular risk, with animal and in vitro data for anti-diabetic and anti-inflammatory effects.
how: Steep 1-2 tsp (or one bag) in 8 oz boiling water 5-10 minutes; drink freely, caffeine-free. Green (unfermented) rooibos has more antioxidants. Apply cooled strong tea to irritated skin or add to a bath.
safety: Extremely safe with almost no known adverse effects. Very rare liver toxicity reports of uncertain causality. Mild estrogenic activity - theoretical caution in estrogen-sensitive conditions at very high intake. May slightly increase iron absorption.
origin: Indigenous to South Africa's Cederberg; the Khoisan have used it for centuries as tea and medicine.

name: African Potato
summary: Hypoxoside converts to rooperol with anti-inflammatory and antiproliferative activity; sterol/sterolin mixtures show immune-modulating effects in clinical studies, and its beta-sitosterol content is linked to relief of BPH symptoms.
how: Standardized beta-sitosterol/sterolin extract (e.g. Moducare): about 20 mg beta-sitosterol plus 0.2 mg sterolin three times daily on an empty stomach. Traditional method boils slices of fresh corm as a decoction.
safety: NOT a substitute for antiretroviral therapy in HIV/AIDS - promoting it as such had tragic consequences in South Africa. May interact with immunosuppressants, diabetes drugs and cholesterol medications. Raw corm potency varies and contains toxic hypoxoside. Avoid in pregnancy/breastfeeding.
origin: A cornerstone plant for Zulu, Sotho and Xhosa healers, used as an immune and urinary tonic.

name: Pelargonium (Umckaloabo)
summary: A Cochrane Review of 10 RCTs concluded Pelargonium sidoides extract EPs 7630 relieves symptoms of acute bronchitis; further reviews support use in sinusitis and the common cold. It is a licensed pharmaceutical in Germany.
how: Standardized root extract EPs 7630 as drops or tablets: adults typically 30 drops or 20 mg three times daily for 7-10 days, started at the first sign of infection.
safety: Rare liver injury - stop if jaundice or dark urine appears. May increase bleeding risk; caution with anticoagulants and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Avoid in severe liver or kidney disease and in pregnancy/breastfeeding. Allergic reactions possible.
origin: Zulu, Basotho and Xhosa healers used the red-brown root for coughs and chest infections.

name: Devil's Claw
summary: Standardized devil's claw extract performed comparably to rofecoxib for low back pain in RCTs, and a Cochrane Review found moderate evidence in osteoarthritis; harpagoside inhibits COX-2 and TNF-alpha pathways.
how: Standardized extract giving 50-100 mg harpagoside daily (roughly 600-1200 mg extract) in 2-3 doses; allow 4-8 weeks. Root tea: 1 tsp in 2 cups water, cold-macerated 8 hours or simmered 15-20 minutes.
safety: May increase stomach acid - avoid with gastric or duodenal ulcers. Interacts with warfarin, digoxin-type heart medications and diabetes drugs. Avoid in pregnancy (may stimulate contractions). Diarrhea and GI upset are common. Choose sustainably sourced product.
origin: Used for centuries by the San and Khoi of the Kalahari for pain, fever and digestive complaints.

name: Buchu
summary: Diosphenol and pulegone show antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity in vitro, with animal effects comparable to indomethacin; European pharmacopoeias recognize buchu for urinary complaints, but human trials are lacking.
how: Tea: steep 1-2 tsp dried leaves in 8 oz boiling water 10 minutes, 2-3 cups daily for urinary support. Tinctures and capsules available; buchu vinegar infuses leaves in apple cider vinegar 2-4 weeks.
safety: Contains pulegone, hepatotoxic in large doses - never exceed recommended amounts. Avoid in pregnancy (abortifacient at high doses) and traditionally avoided during menstruation. May interact with blood thinners. Avoid in severe kidney disease; not for children.
origin: A Khoisan remedy and one of the first Cape medicinal plants exported to Europe in the 17th century.

name: Baobab
summary: Baobab fruit pulp has roughly six times the vitamin C of oranges by weight plus prebiotic soluble fiber; research at Oxford Brookes showed baobab extract significantly reduced the glycemic response to white bread.
how: 1-2 tablespoons fruit powder daily in smoothies, water, yogurt or juice; the tartness is pleasant. Baobab seed oil applied directly to dry or aging skin.
safety: Very safe as a food. High fiber can cause bloating if increased suddenly - build up gradually. Theoretical interaction with medications sensitive to steady vitamin C intake. Commercial powder quality varies; seek fair-trade sources.
origin: The 'Tree of Life' used across sub-Saharan Africa for fever, diarrhea, nutrition and skin care.

name: Moringa
summary: A systematic review documented anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-diabetic and lipid-lowering effects, and a clinical trial in diabetic subjects found significantly reduced fasting glucose after moringa leaf supplementation; the leaves are exceptionally nutrient-dense.
how: 1-2 teaspoons leaf powder daily in food, smoothies or water; fresh leaves cooked like spinach; leaf tea 1 tsp powder in 8 oz hot water 5 minutes. Seed (Ben) oil applied to skin.
safety: Root and root bark contain spirochin and must NOT be consumed (toxic, uterine contractions, abortifacient). Leaves are safe at food doses. May interact with thyroid medications, diabetes drugs and blood pressure medications - it can lower BP. Start small.
origin: Sub-Himalayan in origin but woven into West, East and southern African medicine as 'never die'.

name: African Ginger
summary: South African research identified strong anti-inflammatory activity through COX-1 and COX-2 inhibition, comparable to some NSAIDs, plus in vitro antimalarial activity; siphonochilone is the unique active furanoterpenoid.
how: Only use cultivated material. Fresh rhizome can be chewed or brewed as tea; dried rhizome powder 250-500 mg as tea or capsules. Commercial supply is limited.
safety: Critically endangered - never harvest from the wild. Limited human safety data from formal trials. Avoid in pregnancy. Theoretical interactions with anti-inflammatory drugs and blood thinners.
origin: Among the most valued herbs of Zulu, Swazi and Tsonga healers for coughs, pain and fever.

name: Bitter Leaf
summary: Sesquiterpene lactones show antiparasitic and antimalarial activity in vitro; animal studies show significant blood-sugar lowering, and a Nigerian clinical study found improved glycemic control with adjunctive bitter leaf.
how: Fresh leaf juice: wash, macerate and squeeze leaves, drink 1-2 tablespoons diluted in water. Bitter leaf soup is the common food form. Dried leaf powder 1-2 g in capsules or tea.
safety: Should NOT replace antimalarial drugs. May potentiate blood-sugar-lowering medications - monitor glucose closely. May interact with anticoagulants. Avoid in pregnancy. High doses cause diarrhea and cramps; verify species identification.
origin: Widely used in Nigerian, Cameroonian and Congolese medicine; wild apes self-medicate with it.

name: Neem
summary: Neem chewing sticks show antimicrobial activity against oral pathogens and are WHO-recognized for oral hygiene; leaf extracts show hypoglycemic effects in animals and limited human studies.
how: Leaf tea: 5-10 dried leaves steeped 10 minutes (very bitter). Neem oil externally only, diluted ~1:10 in carrier oil for fungal infections or acne. Twigs used as chewing sticks.
safety: Neem oil must NEVER be ingested - it is internally toxic and has caused deaths in children. Not safe internally for infants or young children. Avoid in pregnancy (documented anti-fertility effects). May interact with diabetes drugs, immunosuppressants and lithium; can lower blood sugar sharply.
origin: South Asian in origin, adopted across the Sahel and East Africa as 'the tree of 40 cures'.

name: Shea Butter
summary: Shea's triterpenes (lupeol, amyrins) show anti-inflammatory effects comparable to mild topical steroids in preclinical work, and clinical dermatology observations support it as an emollient for eczema and dermatitis; cinnamic esters give mild UV protection (SPF 3-6).
how: Apply unrefined (Grade A) shea butter directly to skin; for eczema or dermatitis apply 2-3 times daily. For muscle and joint pain, warm it and massage into the area. Can be blended with essential oils.
safety: Very safe topically. Rare allergic reactions (occasionally linked to latex or tree nut allergy). Can be comedogenic - not ideal for acne-prone skin. Quality varies enormously; refined shea loses most bioactives.
origin: Used for millennia across the West African shea belt for skin, wounds, joints and newborn care.

name: Hoodia
summary: The steroidal glycoside P57 suppressed appetite in animals, but a Unilever human trial showed only modest effects plus concerning liver side effects, and development was abandoned in 2008. Human weight-loss evidence is unconvincing.
how: Not confidently recommendable given weak evidence and rampant product adulteration. Traditional use involved chewing fresh stem flesh, impractical outside the Kalahari.
safety: Potential liver toxicity identified in trials. May affect blood sugar and interact with diabetes medications. Many commercial products contain no real Hoodia. CITES-listed. Avoid in pregnancy, breastfeeding and children; no long-term safety data.
origin: San hunters of the Kalahari chewed the stem to blunt hunger and thirst on long tracking hunts.

name: Elderberry / Elderflower
summary: A landmark RCT found elderberry extract shortened influenza duration by about 4 days versus placebo, and a 2019 meta-analysis confirmed substantially reduced upper respiratory symptoms; anthocyanins inhibit viral entry and replication.
how: Syrup: simmer 1 cup dried berries in 3 cups water 45 minutes, strain, add 1 cup honey once cooled below 110F. 1 tbsp daily for prevention, every 2-3 hours when ill. Elderflower tea: 2 tsp in 8 oz water 10-15 minutes.
safety: NEVER eat raw berries, leaves, bark or stems - cyanogenic glycosides cause vomiting, diarrhea and potential cyanide toxicity; always cook. Theoretical cytokine concern in autoimmune disease or severe COVID. May interact with immunosuppressants, diuretics and diabetes drugs.
origin: Called the 'medicine chest of the people' across Celtic, Germanic and Slavic folk traditions.

name: Hawthorn Berry
summary: A Cochrane Review of 14 trials found hawthorn extract significantly improved exercise tolerance and reduced fatigue and breathlessness in chronic heart failure; the large SPICE trial showed 39.7% fewer sudden cardiac deaths in a prespecified subgroup.
how: Standardized extract (WS 1442 or LI 132) 160-900 mg daily; allow 6-12 weeks. Berry tea: 1-2 tsp crushed dried berries steeped 15-20 minutes. Tincture 1-2 mL three times daily.
safety: Do not self-treat heart failure - use only under medical supervision and never as a replacement for standard therapy. May potentiate digoxin (dose monitoring required) and blood pressure drugs. Avoid combining with CNS depressants. Dizziness, GI upset, palpitations possible.
origin: Sacred in Celtic tradition; adopted as a heart tonic in 19th-century Irish and Germanic practice.

name: Lemon Balm
summary: 600 mg of lemon balm extract increased calmness and alertness in a randomized crossover study, and topical 1% cream reduced healing time and recurrence of herpes cold sores in RCTs, comparable to acyclovir in some trials.
how: Tea: 1.5-4.5 g fresh or dried leaf in 8 oz boiling water 5-10 minutes, 2-4 cups daily. Cold sores: apply standardized cream 2-4 times daily starting at the first tingle. Cognitive use: 300-600 mg standardized extract.
safety: Very safe generally. May inhibit TSH and interfere with thyroid function - caution with hypothyroidism or thyroid medication. May enhance sedatives and interact with HIV medications. Avoid high doses in pregnancy.
origin: Carmelite nuns made 'Carmelite water' from it in the 14th century; Charlemagne ordered it in every monastery garden.

name: Calendula
summary: In a Journal of Clinical Oncology trial, calendula ointment significantly outperformed trolamine at preventing radiation dermatitis in breast cancer patients; reviews confirm it promotes granulation tissue, collagen synthesis and angiogenesis.
how: Infused oil: cover dried petals with olive oil, steep 4-6 weeks, strain, apply as needed; add beeswax 1:4 for a salve. Mouth rinse: 1-2 tsp petals in 8 oz boiling water, cooled. Commercial creams widely available.
safety: Allergic reactions possible with Asteraceae sensitivity. Avoid oral use in pregnancy (emmenagogue concern); topical use is considered safe. Do not apply to deep or seriously infected wounds without medical evaluation.
origin: A fixture of medieval monastic physic gardens; used as a wound poultice in the Civil War and WWI.

name: Arnica
summary: A systematic review found topical arnica gel as effective as topical ibuprofen for hand osteoarthritis, and a randomized trial showed reduced bruising and pain after rhinoplasty; helenalin inhibits the inflammatory transcription factor NF-kB.
how: Apply standardized arnica gel or cream to bruises, sprains and sore muscles 2-4 times daily, or use diluted tincture as a compress. Topical use only.
safety: NEVER take arnica internally outside homeopathic dilutions - helenalin is cardiotoxic and can be fatal. Do not apply to broken skin or open wounds, or near eyes and mucous membranes. Allergic contact dermatitis is common with prolonged use; avoid with Asteraceae allergy.
origin: A staple of Germanic, Swiss and Austrian alpine folk medicine for falls, bruises and sprains.

name: Comfrey
summary: A large RCT showed comfrey root ointment was significantly superior to placebo for acute ankle sprains, with pain reduction comparable to topical diclofenac; allantoin and rosmarinic acid drive tissue repair and anti-inflammatory effects.
how: Topical only. Apply PA-controlled commercial cream or ointment to the affected area 2-4 times daily for sprains, strains, bruises and back pain. Limit to 4-6 weeks per year (some authorities say 10 consecutive days).
safety: NEVER take comfrey internally - pyrrolizidine alkaloids cause fatal veno-occlusive liver disease and deaths have occurred; oral products are banned in the US. Do not apply to broken skin (PAs are absorbed). Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Root has more PAs than leaf.
origin: English folk medicine's 'knitbone', poulticed onto fractures and sprains for centuries.

name: Mullein
summary: A pediatric trial found herbal ear drops containing mullein, garlic, calendula and St. John's Wort matched anesthetic drops for ear pain in acute otitis media; mullein saponins are expectorant and verbascoside is anti-inflammatory.
how: Leaf tea: 1-2 tsp dried leaf steeped 10-15 minutes, strained through cloth or coffee filter, 2-3 cups daily. Ear oil: flowers infused in olive oil 2-4 weeks, a few warm drops in the ear.
safety: Always strain the tea - fine leaf hairs irritate the throat. Do not use ear oil if the eardrum is perforated; ear infections need medical evaluation, especially in children. Seeds are mildly toxic. Do not smoke the leaves. Limited formal safety data.
origin: Featured in Bald's Leechbook and Hildegard von Bingen's writings for coughs and earache.

name: Plantain Herb
aka: Plantago major, P. lanceolata, waybread, ribwort
summary: A randomized clinical trial showed Plantago major extract significantly accelerated wound healing, and Plantago lanceolata syrup is EMA-approved for cough with the common cold; aucubin and allantoin drive tissue repair.
how: First aid: chew or crush a fresh leaf onto insect bites, stings or minor cuts - itch relief within minutes. Tea: 1-2 tsp dried leaf steeped 10 minutes for cough or as a mouth rinse. Salve: leaves infused in oil with beeswax.
safety: Very safe; rare allergic reactions. Harvest only from areas free of pesticides and animal traffic. May mildly lower blood pressure; theoretical lithium interaction via diuretic effect. Plantain allergy may cross-react with psyllium.
origin: One of the nine sacred herbs of the Anglo-Saxon Nine Herbs Charm, known as waybread.

name: Horsetail
summary: One of the richest plant sources of bioavailable silica: a randomized trial found horsetail extract significantly improved nail brittleness, and another found diuretic effects comparable to hydrochlorothiazide without major electrolyte disturbance.
how: Decoction (needed to extract silica): simmer 2-4 tsp dried horsetail in 8 oz water 15-20 minutes, 2-3 cups daily up to 6 weeks. Capsules 300 mg three times daily; allow 2-3 months for nails.
safety: Contains thiaminase which destroys vitamin B1 - supplement B1 or limit to 6 weeks then break. CRITICAL: field horsetail is safe but marsh horsetail (E. palustre) is toxic - never wild-harvest without expert ID. Avoid in kidney or heart failure; may interact with diuretics and lithium. Avoid in pregnancy.
origin: Used across Germanic and Celtic folk medicine for urinary complaints and to strengthen bones and nails.

name: Marshmallow Root
summary: Up to 35% mucilage polysaccharides coat and soothe irritated mucous membranes; a clinical study showed marshmallow root syrup significantly reduced dry cough severity, and a randomized trial found relief of GERD symptoms.
how: Cold infusion (best preserves mucilage): soak 1 tbsp dried root in 8 oz cold water 4-8 hours or overnight, strain and drink. Hot version: steep 1-2 tsp in hot, not boiling, water 10 minutes. 2-3 cups daily for cough and sore throat.
safety: Very safe. The mucilage can slow or reduce absorption of oral medications - take it at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after other drugs. May lower blood sugar; monitor if diabetic. Insufficient pregnancy data. Rare allergy.
origin: Used since antiquity; the original marshmallow confection was a medicinal lozenge made from this root.

name: Meadowsweet
summary: Meadowsweet contains natural salicylates (aspirin was first derived from it) alongside tannins and mucilage that appear gastroprotective, and studies confirm anti-inflammatory and stomach-soothing effects; the EMA recognizes it for mild joint pain and colds.
how: Tea: steep 2-4 tsp dried flowering tops and leaves in 8 oz hot (not boiling) water 10-15 minutes; 2-3 cups daily for pain, fever or heartburn. Tincture 2-4 mL three times daily.
safety: Avoid with aspirin or salicylate sensitivity. Do not give to children under 16 (precautionary Reye's syndrome concern). May interact with blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs; stop before surgery and use cautiously with NSAIDs. Avoid in active peptic ulcer and in large doses during pregnancy.
origin: One of the three most sacred Druid herbs; its old genus name Spiraea gave aspirin its name.

name: Feverfew
summary: A landmark BMJ crossover trial showed feverfew significantly reduced migraine frequency and severity, and a Cochrane Review of 5 RCTs found mixed but generally supportive results for migraine prevention; parthenolide inhibits platelet serotonin release and NF-kB.
how: Standardized extract with 0.2-0.4% parthenolide, 50-100 mg daily, or freeze-dried leaf capsules 50-125 mg daily; or 2-3 fresh leaves daily. Allow 4-6 weeks. Preventive only, not for acute attacks.
safety: Avoid in pregnancy (may stimulate uterine contractions). Chewing fresh leaves causes mouth ulcers. Abrupt withdrawal after long use causes 'post-feverfew syndrome' (rebound headache, anxiety, stiffness) - taper. Interacts with blood thinners, antiplatelet drugs and CYP-metabolized medications. Asteraceae allergy; not for children.
origin: Medieval European folk medicine's 'fever reducer', taken for headaches and women's complaints.
